analytic.title: Conservative Design with High-Performance COTS Architectures -Beyond Traditional Approaches

div.p: Safety-critical industrial systems are subject to many stringent requirements, including non-functional design constraints that are essential for robustness, reliability, and safety. System timing is often treated as an afterthought, even though data age, race conditions, or missed deadlines can affect functional safety. This challenge has been addressed in realtime system design, but the situation has worsened in recent system designs. Many applications require high performance to achieve behavioral safety goals, i.e., safety of intended functionality, using complex heterogeneous architectures with multi-level memory, interconnected chiplets, and accelerators based on the latest technologies. Machine learning applications in factory automation, robotics, and autonomous systems are important examples. The timing of such architectures is heavily influenced by the physical effects of temperature control and chip variations, including aging, leading to even more complex chip-specific software execution timing. The paper shows that identical chips differ in their timing behavior, and that most of the timing variation of a single chip can be effectively modeled using additive white Gaussian noise. We explain how such timing behavior can be exploited in high-assurance design for safety and reliability, following established reliability analysis, test, and redundancy techniques.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The challenges of performing system-level test to achieve comprehensive test coverage in complex hardware-software systems have been the subject of extensive research in recent years. The demand for agile software development practices has further accentuated the need for innovative testing methodologies. In agile software development, the adoption of online testing methodologies has gained significant prominence due to their ability to ensure continuous evaluation and verification of system functionality [1]. However, in the quest to ensure functional correctness, a critical aspect often receives less attention: the timing behavior of these systems.

The inherent complexities of modern heterogeneous multicore processors, including multi-level memory hierarchies, chiplets, and accelerators, introduce uncertainties in timing behavior. Obtaining response time bounds and verifying them is a challenging task, as architecture-related factors such as arbitration in cache coherency protocols and access to shared resources interact with software effects such as interrupt handling and scheduling policies. As a major factor, physical effects such as on-chip variations, jittered clock frequencies, and varying heat dissipation result in unique timing variations for each chip in a model series. As a result, each individual chip has different timing, even under identical input and environmental conditions. This paper provides examples.

Strictly conservative design with temperature control disabled and fixed lower frequency implemented in established technologies is the typical current choice, but this approach severely limits system performance, likely leading to a loss of competitiveness as high-performance architectures become more controllable, including reliable timing. As we will show in this paper, there is a good opportunity to specifically exploit the properties of machine learning algorithms. This is particularly relevant in emerging applications where realtime systems and embedded software are integral parts of applications ranging from automated manufacturing to autonomous robots. Deterministic timing is often required to ensure the safe and reliable operation of increasingly complex manufacturing robots, evolving from collaborative robots to humanoid robots [2]. This includes a safety risk for human beings nearby if the timing behavior is insufficient.

div.head: Contribution:
div.p: We demonstrate the impact of physical effects on system timing behavior and highlight the need to consider physical design and chip-specific timing behavior to avoid unsafe system designs. We present an experiment using a neural network-based perception pipeline to empathize design challenges related to temperature control and chip variation. We also show that response times vary randomly within and between test series, but can be approximated by additive white Gaussian noise. Finally, we discuss the implications of noisy response time variations for system design and how redundancy and online testing can be used to increase system-level design and test confidence in timing.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. We give a brief background on real-time systems in Section II, which is continued by related work in Section III. Then, we demonstrate the limitation of tests in real-time systems, beginning with the chip-individual temperature limits in Section V. Thereafter, we investigate the repeatability of timing within a test series (see Section VI) and between test series (see Section VII). This is followed by a discussion in Section VIII dealing with the implications of our findings including aging. Finally, we summarize our work in Section IX.

div.head: II. BACKGROUND
div.p: A real-time system is a computing system performing a set of tasks T . A task receives input data when it begins and responds with an output when it completes. The correctness of the provided output depends on the logical correctness as well as on its timing. Timing concerns include schedulability, i.e., sufficient performance to fully execute all implemented applications, and response times, i.e., the adherence to maximum latencies, formulated as deadlines. Deadlines are defined at design time and are then imposed on the task set. For any task T i in the task set T , it is necessary to meet its deadline D i to guarantee that the system complies with its timing requirements. The execution time C i of a task T i varies, depending on the input, the control flow path the task takes, and the inner state of the underlying hardware. For a finite set of inputs, there is an upper bound on the execution time C i called worst-case execution time (WCET), which is denoted as C i . Naturally, the WCET C i of a task must be less than or equal to its deadline D i , i.e., C i ≤ D i . Otherwise, the task would execute longer than its deadline, thus violating its timing constraints. However, depending on the number of computational resources, e.g., cores, the number of tasks, and the scheduling algorithm used, tasks may have to wait for computational resources or get preempted during computation by a higher priority task. The time it takes a task T i to respond, measured from its start to its end, is called the response time R i . If a task has to wait to complete its computation, the response time R i will exceed its WCET C i . Therefore, the response time analysis takes into account the scheduling algorithm and the WCET to calculate the worst-case response time (WCRT) R i , for which holds C i ≤ R i ≤ D i . Although the response time analysis itself can be quite complex, it can be handled due to comprehensive research and methodologies.

Estimating a sound but tight WCET is challenging due to unknowns in the chip implementation and uncertainties in the interaction of chip components. As a key factor, physical effects and dynamic control of temperature and clock frequency further complicate obtaining a sound timing bound. Overestimating the WCET results in wasted size, weight, power, and increased costs or even the system design not being operational due to lack of performance capabilities. Two different approaches can be utilized to obtain an accurate WCET by analysis.

1. Optimize the model. If both the system behavior and the application control flow are fully known, worst-case timings can be derived. Modeling the system using upper bounds on internal timings, e.g., memory access times, usually results in an overly pessimistic and overestimated WCET. Instead, modeling the system probabilistically, i.e., using random variables for timings, allows us to relate a WCET to a probability of occurrence. Consequently, the level of pessimism can be adjusted to align with the desired level of safety. However, modern multi-core processors exhibit many complex protocols, internal scheduling mechanisms, and races, which are often not disclosed. Moreover, access to shared resources, e.g., caches, by concurrently running tasks alters the system state constantly, and races among the tasks impact their timing behavior. Even worse, these effects are increasingly dependent on the specific device physics and manufacturing variations, which is further limiting the accuracy of a general device model.

2. Enforce predictability. As it is challenging to model the complete system precisely, another approach is to ensure that the system behaves in a more predictable manner. Consequently, complex features such as simultaneous multithreading, out-of-order execution, or speculative execution are often disabled. Physical effects can be constrained by disabling temperature and frequency control and utilizing older technologies with less variable behavior. While such a system can be analyzed with greater accuracy, this approach is accompanied by a significant performance penalty.

Due to the difficulties in obtaining a WCET by formal analysis, test-based and measurement-based approaches are applied. In this context, the execution time C i is measured N -times forming an execution time trace D T = {C i,1 , . . . , C i,N }. The maximum of that trace can then be increased by a relative safety margin M (typically 1 > M > 0) to account for uncertainties or unknowns. So the WCET estimation C i ′ is given by

This method is notable for its simplicity. However, it is also associated with significant drawbacks. 1. Repeatability. Tests can only show the presence of upsets, not their absence. Instead, formal analysis can provide proof, and thus the approaches differ in their provided guarantees. Additionally, a timing test is not entirely reproducible due to the random nature of the data. As a result, the test's outcome may not be consistent, and may only converge to a reproducible distribution over time. This introduces a degree of uncertainty into the test.

2. Variance Each chip is a unique unit and is subject to manufacturing variations, although it corresponds to the functional bounds of the chip design. These variations accumulate over time due to semiconductor-inherent aging causing transistor delay to increase [3]. Consequently, one-time tests have a limited significance for the timing behavior throughout the lifetime of a system.

3. Number of measurements. Safety standards demand a tremendous level of reliability. Depending on the specific standard one error in the range of 10 6 h (approx. 114 years) to 10 9 h (114, 000 years) are acceptable. However, measuring for such a long time is infeasible. Nevertheless, measuring only a few samples is not sufficient to guarantee safety. It is possible to extrapolate the data in order to reduce the number of tests needed, e.g., using extreme value theory. However, whether this is a safe practice is subject to ongoing discussions within the real-time community [4].

4. Target scenario. Tests are only significant if conducted on the target platform using the final software and the specific operating parameters. Since changing anything may lead to a different timing behavior, testing is required after each update. Furthermore, a different chip from the same series can exhibit a different timing behavior. Therefore, one chip may fulfill the timing requirements for one scenario while violating the requirements of another scenario, and vice versa for a different chip. This further increases the cost of testing.

In summary, the validation of the timing behavior to ensure compliance with safety standards is a challenging task. While formal analysis approaches are susceptible to uncertain or even erroneous models and burdened by significant performance penalties, test-based methods present potential safety risks due to their limited significance caused by physical uncertainties. Tackling this challenge, we aim to increase the level of confidence in test-based methods by exploiting redundancy.

div.head: III. RELATED WORK
div.p: It is comprehensible that different tasks have different execution times. However, that the execution time jitters among multiple runs of the same, stateless task is less intuitive. In multi-task systems timing variations were found to be software-related like context switches and interrupt handling further affected by hardware states, e.g., caches and memory states. Later with the rise of multi-core processors, concurrently running applications on different cores competing for computation resources were the reason for even larger timing variations [5], [6] This led to many different approaches aiming to get rid of timing outliers [7]. Some restricted the memory bandwidth for certain cores to prohibit concurrent access [8], and some altered the execution model to achieve temporal isolation [9], and others proposed heuristics to estimate the maximum of concurrency which can be used safely [10]. While some researchers designed time-predictable multi-core hardware [11], others focused on the opposite: designing time-randomized hardware [12]. However such hardware was not used widely outside academia. In contrast to commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) multi-core processors, randomized hardware could be well analyzed using models from the extreme value theory (EVT) [13]. Thereafter, even COTS hardware was studied using EVT [14], but causing ongoing discussions [4] and inspiring papers showing that the necessary assumption of independent and identical distributed execution times is not always valid [15].

On the one hand, recent technology nodes and more sophisticated hardware control like core-individual frequency and temperature control [16], as well as the introduction of chiplets and hybrid architecture [17], further aggravates the determinism of execution timings. On the other, controlling modern collaborative robots and future humanoid robots requires complex control loops with strict timing requirements incorporating perception pipelines based on neural networks. This dilemma demands realistic and straightforward design and test solutions, enabling the safe operation of highperformance platforms without compromising time to market. Though also the neural network community proposes "realtime" solutions, they associate it more with faster inference time or online learning as with timing guarantees and safety aspects. Furthermore, their safety challenges are about validating the functional correctness including vulnerabilities against malicious attacks [18].

In this paper, we provide an extended explanation for the timing variance and present statistical evidence in a use case. We observed that the physical effects of high-performance chip control, which have largely been ignored in previous work on real-time systems, are an important source of timing randomness, amplified by their impact on hardware races and concurrent software effects. Due to the large number of such concurrency effects in modern devices, they can accumulate towards rare large outliers. As a positive aspect of such random-induced timing behavior, we can use established techniques of redundancy to mask such outliers.

div.head: IV. REAL-TIME TESTBED
div.p: We begin with describing our real-time testbed used for the experiments in the following sections. Our testbed consists of one or multiple system under tests (SUTs) and a dedicated workstation, which are connected via Gbit-Ethernet (cf. Fig. 1a). The SUTs execute an application under controlled conditions and measure its timing behavior and relevant system data, e.g., number of context switches, page faults, temperature, and clock frequency, and send these data in combination with the application's result to the Workstation. On the one hand, the workstation's task is to store these data for later processing. On the other hand, it also controls the test procedure of the SUTs by sending input data periodically to trigger the execution of the application. To enable deterministic test repetitions, a set of prerecorded inputs is utilized by the input generator. Both, the SUTs and the workstation employ UDP/IP sockets for data transmission, in addition the workstation employs multi-cast to facilitate the connection of multiple SUTs at the same time. The workstation also monitors the elapsed time to monitor the Ethernet connection. In our experiments, we use two embedded multi-core Intel i5-1240p platforms as SUTs. On top of these run Linux with PREEMPT_RT patch, configured for real-time load. This includes running the application with a high priority in the round-robin scheduling queue (SCHED RR) and disabling Linux's real-time throttling by setting the kernel parameters sched rt runtime us and sched rt period us appropriately.

On the software side we deploy a self-trained, YOLOv5based [19] neural network application for object detection and identification. The application starts whenever it receives input data, in this case, a JPEG-compressed input frame. It comprises three distinct pipeline stages, which are illustrated in Fig. 1b. In PRE the application pre-processes the input image, this includes decoding as well as resizing the image to 640 × 640 pixels to fit the neural network. Next, the neural network executes and performs the perception (MODEL). The raw result is then post-processed in the POST-stage. We refer to all stages combined as FULL. Thereafter, the result is transmitted back to the workstation in combination with measured execution times for each stage and overall gathered system data. After the test sequence ends, the measured timing behavior and system data can be analyzed. Note that, we always use a period of 100 ms between sending two images, and thus between two samples.

At last, we want to clarify a few terms. During each experiment, the YOLOv5 application is executed multiple times. For each iteration, an input image is sent to the application and the response time is measured. A single response time measurement is called sample and consecutive samples forming a trace. During a trace the application initiates only once but may process numerous input images, thereby generating numerous samples. Upon completion of the application, the trace is terminated. When the application starts again a new trace begins, and a set of traces is called ensemble.

div.head: V. EXPERIMENT I
div.p: In the first experiment, we demonstrate the tremendous impact of environmental conditions and device physics on the performance of our YOLOv5 neural network application.

div.head: A. Impact of physical effects
div.p: Real-time tests often assume a constant clock frequency with dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) disabled. This assumption enormously reduces complexity, as the complexity of modeling clock frequency shifts can be avoided. Nevertheless, more recent architectures implement DVFS control directly in hardware and do not accept commands from the operating system but only hints [16]. While reducing software designer control, this feature supports maximum performance while still respecting chip-individual temperature limits and thus avoids failure or premature aging.

Although environmental factors such as temperature and humidity can influence clock frequency, they are typically excluded from timing models for simplicity. Chip control reduces voltage and clock frequency to prevent self-damage due to overheating when the temperature reaches a critical point. However, heat can also affect the timing behavior within the permitted temperature range, as the data trace of the testbed in Fig. 2 demonstrates. While the upper half of the figure presents the response time of our YOLOv5 application, the lower part displays the clock frequency and package temperature of the chip. Though the CPU's critical temperature for our Intel i5-1240p is specified at 105°C, the frequency almost halves when the chip reaches 90°C, and consequently causes a massive, peak in response time despite identical iterations. Following the second peak, the chip reaches a temperature of 95°C and continues to operate at its specified frequency. At this point, the response time stabilizes at a constant level. This behavior illustrates the significance of environmental considerations and temperature control for timing.

div.head: B. Impact of on-chip variations
div.p: It is commonly assumed that the timing behavior of a chip should be identical on all chips of the same series. But because of on-chip variations, which become more prominent with the use of more advanced technology nodes in semiconductor manufacturing [3], this assumption can be misleading. Furthermore, the effects of aging can also influence performance, thereby increasing the discrepancies in timing behavior over time. These additional impacts are rarely considered, yet they should be included in timing tests and in-field monitoring to prevent unexpected failures.

The impact of on-chip variations and chip-individual temperature control can be observed in the following data trace (see Fig. 3), which was obtained simultaneously under equal conditions to the previous one. In this instance, another Intel i5-1240p chip from the same series was utilized. This chip exhibits a substantially different thermal behavior, wherein no timing outlier occurs though the CPU reaches 92°C. These examples demonstrate the necessity of characterizing each chip over the full temperature range for its timing behavior. Both parts of this first experiment show that the chip's temperature control is a dominant factor in determining a predictable timing behavior and that each chip must be speedgraded over the entire temperature range to account for anomalies and chip variations.

div.head: VI. EXPERIMENT II
div.p: The example from the last section demonstrated the impact of on-chip variations and physical effects on the chip's timing behavior for the range of typically permitted environmental conditions. But also under constant environmental conditions timing is affected by physical effects. We show this using the presented testbed and our YOLOv5 neural network application (see Fig. 1a and Fig. 1b). To avoid timing variations due to changing input data, we feed the same input image into the neural network and measure the response time after each execution. This is in contrast to the initial experiment where we used a stream of consecutive input images to provide a more realistic use case. Against intuition the experiment does not exhibit a perfectly constant response time, instead, it seems to be superimposed by noise as can be seen in Fig. 4. In the following, we will apply statistical techniques to investigate the hypothesis that the observed fluctuations in response time are due to noise.

A noisy response time sample R at an iteration i, which origins from a constant expected value µ but is superimposed by a noise distribution ϵ can be described using a standard model for additive noise from signal processing theory:

Fig. 4: Response time trace of our YOLOv5 application using always the same input image to achieve a response time as repeatable as possible. Instead of a single constant line, the trace shows a broader distribution and some outliers approx. at iteration 60,000.

The subsequent step is to further characterize ϵ(i) in order to investigate its origin. Therefore, we test if it is subject to repeating patterns, by calculating the autocorrelation acf and the power spectral density psd (see Fig. 5a and Fig. 5b) As a brief recap, autocorrelation provides a quantitative estimation in the range of [-1; 1] of the similarity between a data series with itself shifted by a lag k. If the data series is compared to itself without being shifted, i.e., lag k = 0, it is maximally similar to itself and therefore reaches the maximum value of 1. Conversely, if the signal does not show any similarity at a lag k, its value is equal to 0. The psd shows the intensity of the signal, i.e., trace, for the frequency domain. If the signal peaks at a frequency, e.g., at 1 Hz, it states that the signal shows a periodicity to 1 Hz.

The observed autocorrelation (Fig. 5a) appears to be approximately a Dirac delta function, commonly observed in the autocorrelation of white noise. Additionally, the psd for white noise is approximately constant, as each frequency should occur with equal incidence (Fig. 5b).

However, the psd rises for low frequencies indicating the presence of a slowly repeating pattern. Consequently, we conducted an investigation into the source of this phenomenon and identified a tiny sawtooth wave in the response time noise, superimposed with a large level of noise. We traced this down to some software effects in the external JPEG library used for decoding the input images.

These results demonstrate that response times vary over iterations even when using constant input data and ideal temperature conditions. Moreover, the majority of these fluctuations occur randomly and can be adequately represented by white noise. This contrasts with traditional methodologies that assume complete repeatability.

div.head: VII. EXPERIMENT III
div.p: Even if a single iteration is not repeatable, deterministically caused timing variations could still occur, as a result of the underlying mechanics of the platform, e.g., cache effects. Consequently, these variations would be repeatable Power spectral density (b) Spectral power density of the noise term ϵ(i). with respect to a given trace. This would imply that one trace is sufficient to fully characterize the response time, at least for the length of the trace itself. To investigate this, we conducted our final experiment, measuring not one trace but an ensemble, i.e., a set of traces with equal length and image contents. This approach ensures that, after each trace, the application is closed, so the next trace relies on a new instance of the application, which begins from an empty cache. Hence, each trace starts from the same system state and should exhibit the same deterministic timing pattern. We execute 1000 traces with a set of 1000 consecutive input images, leading to 1000 samples per trace. The response time noise of the ensemble is presented in Fig. 7, showing that different input images need a different amount of response time. However, each iteration shows a notable enclosing around its mean caused by lots of variations between the traces. This demonstrates that each trace exhibits its unique response time and is not fully repeatable. Though the overall course is characterized by the input images, the impact on the response time is relatively small.

To further substantiate that repeatability is limited and noise occurs arbitrarily, we calculate the autocorrelation and power spectral density for each iteration of the response time noise shown in Fig. 7. This results in 1000 acf and psd plots, which we combine in a single figure with intervals for the variations (see. Fig. 6). The graphic shows a constant power spectral density and a Dirac delta function for the autocorrelation, suggesting that response time noise between traces equals white noise.

Moreover, Fig. 8a shows that the measured distribution PSD between traces 90% interval 50% interval Mean Fig. 6: The autocorrelation and power spectral density along a single iteration between all 1000 traces. It was conducted for all iterations and then averaged (see mean), 50%, resp. 90%, of all acf , resp. psd, values are within the colored interval. of response time noise can be well approximated using a Gaussian normal distribution. Consequently, the observed timing variations can be modeled conveniently as additive white Gaussian noise. This is the basic model to describe random processes emerging from many underlying random effects with limited variance. In addition, Fig. 8a emphasizes peaks in the timing using extra markers.

Finally, we conducted the same experiment on our second Intel i5-1240p (see Fig. 8b). Its distribution is strikingly similar, exhibiting a slight narrowing at the mean while simultaneously displaying a greater number of peaks. This evidence suggests that both platforms possess an identical internal structure, yet they remain distinct units with their respective response time characteristics.

div.head: VIII. DISCUSSION
div.p: Overall, we did not identify a roadblock to using highperformance COTS platforms in critical applications. The experiments suggest that we can partition the problem into two challenges, chip temperature control and physically induced timing variations.

In the first experiment (Sec. V) we found that the operating temperature is a dominant impact factor for timing. The sharp and sudden temperature control actions in unexpected instances are an obstacle in critical systems design. An elegant approach would involve modifying the chip's temperature control and performing a speed grading of each chip to deal with chip-individual temperature limits and variations among identical chips. As this is not the case at the moment, choosing a conservative design using the base clock frequency is state-of-the-art, even if this is associated with a loss of performance. Addressing the first challenge in semiconductor design, manufacturing, and qualification is worthwhile be-cause the second challenge could successfully be addressed in systems design. The random timing behavior in experiments II and III (Sec. VI and Sec. VII) obviously roots in the interplay of hardware, OS, and application, induced by physical timing variance. All larger computer architectures include a large variety of races, e.g., in cache coherence, core, and memory protocols, where slight variations in physical timing decide on arbitration and execution sequences. The individual race effects are relatively small and largely average out in hundreds of million clock cycles of Linux and the YOLOv5 application. The result is a substantially different timing pattern than reported in earlier work for small synthetic benchmarks showing large repeatable outliers, e.g. [5]. However, even small but random individual race effects may coincide and lead to the observed rare outliers, as seen in Fig. 8b. This is highly relevant for safety-critical applications. But, the good news is that handling rare random effects is known from systems design, and could therefore be addressed by adaptation of established design and test methods. Examples are tests for random timing errors and the use of redundancy to mask timing errors. More research is needed in this direction.

As an example, we suggest the use of redundancy to increase confidence in the system design and to reduce the risk of unexpected upsets, as this is recommended in many industry standards such as IEC 62061 and IEC 61508 and thus is well-established in safety-critical systems and comes with no additional costs. Some work already dealt with redundancy for timing variations [20]- [23]. Diverse hardware is preferred since it avoids the need to show statistical independence to prevent common-cause failures. However, as we verified timing variations occur uniquely and can be well modeled using additive white Gaussian noise and add up to the variations among identical chips. Therefore, also identical chips can be deployed as redundancy, which reduces system development costs and evades choosing two different but similarly fast hardware.

Redundancy not only helps to keep the system operational when facing unexpected upsets but also allows for increased confidence in the design and test. Given statistical independence, testing a second multi-core processor decreases the probability of a failure by square but only doubles the amount of testing, and thus increases the significance of the test substantially while keeping the additional test expenditure low.

The current situation continues to aggravate with more recent, heterogeneous, high-performance multi-core platforms, particularly, when considering the aspect of aging in a decadelong operation under temperature stress [3]. To guarantee a safe timing behavior throughout the lifetime of a system, online monitoring and regular in-field tests become necessary. These can be well combined using redundancy.

A last point is the use of Linux PREEMPT_RT in the experiments. The autocorrelation tests did not reveal any stateful OS behavior that could cause unexpected softwareinduced timing that was not observed in the extended test sequences. We conclude that, if correctly configured, Linux PREEMPT_RT could be used for such applications, provided for software correctness and IT security, which are out of scope of this paper.

div.head: IX. CONCLUSION
div.p: Besides correctness, non-functional timing constraints impact safety and thus must be tested according to safety standards. Though this challenge has been addressed in real-time system design, many assumptions and methods of traditional worst-case timing analysis are no longer applicable for recent high-performance platforms caused by physical effects, onchip variations, and aging.

Generally, using high-performance architecture in safetycritical systems, such as future autonomous robots, is possible if the design considers chip physics and variations. This includes restricting violent interventions of the chip's temperature control by modifying the existing policy and using speed grading over the whole temperature range. Furthermore, larger timing variations induced by coincidence of physically induced race effects from the underlying platform can be handled by exploiting the randomness of these events using redundancy concepts with respect to timing, while increasing the test's confidence.
